ety.text: The etymology of the noun is unknown, but compare Old French gigue (“a fiddle”). The verb is derived from the noun.
Sense 1 is a clipping of gigabyte, while sense 2 is a clipping of giga- (prefix multiplying the unit to which it is attached by one billion).

chain.g: to yawn, gape, long for, desire

ety.text: The noun is derived from Middle English gigg, gigge, gygge (“spinning object; a top”); further origin uncertain, possibly: * from Old Norse [Term?] (compare Danish gig (“a top”), dialectal Norwegian giga (“to shake about”)), from Proto-Germanic *gīganą (“to move, wish, desire”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeyǵʰ-, *gʰeygʰ- (“to yawn, gape, long for, desire”); or * ultimately onomatopoeic. Senses 2–4 are thought to derive from sense 1 (“whipping-top”), but their exact relationship is unclear. The verb is derived from the noun.

From Middle English gig, gigge, gegge, possibly either: * from Old French gigue (“tall, skinny girl”) (modern French gigue), from Old Norse gikkr (“pert person”) (related to Danish gjæk (“fool, jester”), Swedish gäck (“fool, jester; a wag”); see also geck); or * from Middle English gigg, gigge, gygge (“spinning object; a top”) (see etymology 3).
The noun is derived from a clipping of fishgig, fizgig, possibly from Spanish fisga (“harpoon”). The verb is derived from the noun.

senses.d: Originally (music), a performing engagement by a musician or musical group; (by extension, film, television, theater) a job or role for a performer.
ex: I caught one of the Rolling Stones’ first gigs in Richmond.
Hey, when are we gonna get that hotel gig again?

senses.d: Any job, especially one that is freelance or temporary, or done on an on-demand basis.
ex: I had this gig as a file clerk but it wasn’t my style so I left.
That guy’s got a great gig over at the bike shop. He hardly works all day.

senses.d: A demerit received for some infraction of a military deportment or dress code.
ex: I received gigs for having buttons of my uniform undone.

senses.d: To play (a musical instrument) at a gig.
To impose a demerit (on someone) for an infraction of a military deportment or dress code.
ex: His sergeant gigged him for an unmade bunk.

senses.d: To engage in a musical performance, act in a theatre production, etc.
ex: The Rolling Stones were gigging around Richmond at the time.

senses.d: To work at any job, especially one that is freelance or temporary, or done on an on-demand basis.
Any unit of measurement having the SI prefix giga-.
A top which is made to spin by tying a piece of string around it and then throwing it so that the string unwinds rapidly; a whipping-top.
A person with an odd appearance; also, a foolish person.
Fun; frolics.
A fanciful impulse; a whim; also, a joke.
ex: I muſt goe ſee him preſently, / For this is ſuch a gig: for certaine Gentlemen / The Fiend rides on a Fiddleſticke.

senses.d: A small, narrow, open boat carried in a larger ship, and used for transportation between the ship and the shore, another vessel, etc.
ex: The captain's gig still lies before ye whole and sound, / It shall carry all o' we.

senses.d: A similar rowing boat or sailboat, especially one used for racing; specifically, a six-oared sea rowing boat commonly found in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly.
A two-wheeled carriage drawn by a single horse.
ex: While Sir William was with them, Mr. Collins devoted his mornings to driving him out in his gig, and shewing him the country; […]

senses.d: To make a joke, often condescendingly, at the expense of (someone); to make fun of.
ex: His older cousin was just gigging him about being in love with that girl from school.

senses.d: Sometimes followed by it: to ride in a gig (“a two-wheeled carriage drawn by a single horse”).
A frivolous, playful, or wanton young woman; a giglet or giglot.
Synonym of fishgig or fizgig (“a spear with a barb on the end of it, used for catching fish, frogs, or other small animals”).
To spear (fish, etc.) with a gig or fizgig.
To catch or fish with a gig or fizgig.

From Ancient Greek γιγαντικός (gigantikós), ultimately from γίγας (gígas, “giant”). According to the Poly-Olbion project coined by Michael Drayton in 1612.

senses.d: Very large.
ex: It is in solitude that the imagination exercises its gigantic power; and where are a woman's feelings nurtured but in solitude?

senses.d: Excellent; very good or exciting.
ex: This band is going to be gigantic.

senses.d: In the manner of a giant.
